newsitem.title: PERU: Peru clears rats, puts hostage trauma behind it.
newsitem.headline: Peru clears rats, puts hostage trauma behind it.

text.p: Clearing rats out of the filthy, burned-out Japanese ambassador's home and giving thanks for renewed peace, Peru sought on Tuesday to put its four-month hostage trauma behind it and return to normal life.

But memories of the spectacular military strike against Marxist rebels one week ago were pervasive, as various church services were held around Lima in honour of the 71 hostages who escaped safely and one captive and two commandos who died.
"The experience has been hard," said a solemn-faced Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi at a Mass in the energy and mines ministry, which he also heads.

But he added: "The anguish is over and today, just as in other opportunities we gathered to seek the freedom of the hostages, we join together in thanks to the Supreme Creator for hearing our prayers."
Families of the two hostages and 27 soldiers recovering from the most serious injuries received in the battle kept up their bedside vigils at clinics around the capital.

"We're all praying for those who died and those still in the hospitals," said flower-seller Lourdes Vasquez, who has kept a candle at her stall since last Tuesday. "Peru can restart its life, go forward again, but no one will forget."

There was little public attention focused on the 14 Marxist rebels who stormed the residence Dec. 17, held the building and world attention for 126 days, then died in a 16-minute hail of gunfire and explosions.

Many local media mention only the "three victims" of the raid, with barely a reference to the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) deaths. Most media refer to the MRTA members as deluded "terrorist criminals."

In his speech, Pandolfi also ignored the rebels. "Sadly, at the end three precious lives were lost," he said, adding that the government had stood firm against "the terrorist blackmail to free from jail criminals who had insanely caused so much pain and damage to our country."

Although MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa and second-in-command Rolly Rojas have been buried in shantytown cemeteries, the other 12 rebels' families are still searching for the bodies. Their claims that they were secretly buried or disposed of have won little space in the mainly pro-government media.

President Alberto Fujimori's government has moved quickly to deny reports that two of the rebels were captured alive and executed during the raid. Those reports threatened to tarnish the acclaim Peru has received from around the world for a military strike likened to Israel's legendary 1976 raid to free hijack victims in Entebbe, Uganda.
Local human rights groups have pledged to help the MRTA members' families find and exhume the corpses and to investigate the execution charges.

Although Fujimori's personal popularity has soared on his defeat of the MRTA hostage-takers, a new poll in Lima showed that more than half of Peruvians still oppose a reelection bid by the president for a third term in 2000.

In a letter to Fujimori published in the daily Expreso in Spanish, U.S. President Bill Clinton praised his Peruvian counterpart for "sending a clear message to the whole world of firmness in the face of terrorism."
Clinton also thanked Fujimori for his "great perseverance" in first seeking a peaceful solution and sent his "profound sympathy" to the families of the judge and two soldiers killed.
Around the destroyed diplomatic compound in the upscale district of San Isidro, authorities began a campaign of cleaning up and "de-ratting."

Hundreds, and sometimes thousands, of journalists had camped outside the compound since Dec. 17. Inside, rotting food and rubbish attracted mice and rats who tormented the hostages and later started to bother nearby residents.
